explanation: The troposphere reaches only about 8 to 18 km up, lowest over the poles and highest over the tropics, yet it holds about three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass.

claims.text: Almost all weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.
The stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere lie above the troposphere and hold little weather.
The troposphere extends from the surface to about 8 km over the poles and about 18 km over the tropics.
The troposphere holds about three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Sources agree that the troposphere is thickest at the equator and thinnest at the poles, but the exact figures differ somewhat. Equator: NOAA puts the top of the troposphere at about 18 to 20 km. It is 11-12 miles (18-20 km) high at the equator. NASA gives a slightly lower range of about 17 to 18 km. Poles: NOAA gives about 6 km, and NASA gives about 7 km. UCAR notes that the poles are lowest in winter, when the tropopause can drop to around 7 km.

claimResults.note: Figures attributed to NOAA, NASA and UCAR (Tier A); the arXiv preprints in the list are not relied on. The tropics figure fits (17 to 20 km by source), but no Tier A source gives 8 km for the poles (NOAA about 6 km, NASA and UCAR about 7 km), and the summary reports that the figures differ. A conflict fails the claim as written (section 9.5.2).
